issues.legal_issue: A parliamentary law on a subject already assigned to Parliament for the State does not require fresh state concurrence each time Parliament legislates on that subject.
material_facts: The applicable presidential order extended the relevant Union List entries, including banking and jurisdiction over courts concerning Union List matters, to the State.

The constitutional framework applicable to the State gave Parliament exclusive power over the extended Union List subjects and did not require further state concurrence for each parliamentary enactment on them.
issues.conclusion: Once a subject in the Union List has been extended to the State by presidential order, Parliament may legislate on that subject without obtaining fresh state concurrence for each law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 370(1)(b) and (d), as applied through the 1954 Presidential Order and subsequent orders, govern the extension of constitutional subjects and provisions to the State. The court relied on Sampat Prakash v. State of Jammu & Kashmir, (1969) 2 SCR 365, and Puranlal Lakhanpal v. President of India, (1962) 1 SCR 688, including their holdings on the continuing operation of Article 370 and the breadth of the power to modify constitutional provisions. A constitutional amendment and an ordinary parliamentary law are governed by distinct constitutional language; extension of a legislative field does not require renewed concurrence whenever Parliament legislates within it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_parliamentar: A party challenges whether Parliament could make a law applicable in a specially governed State.
predicates.relevant_legislative_subject_already_ext: A valid constitutional order has already assigned the law's relevant legislative subject to Parliament for that State.

issues.definition: When a parliamentary law is challenged in a specially governed State and its relevant subject has already been assigned to Parliament there, the law operates without fresh state concurrence.

issues.legal_issue: A law whose substance is the recovery of debts owed to banks falls within Parliament's legislative authority over banking, including measures that enable recovery outside the ordinary court process.
material_facts: The challenged law allowed secured creditors to enforce security interests, including by taking possession of secured assets and selling or assigning them to recover debts.
The law also allowed creditors to take over business management, appoint managers, and require persons owing money to the borrower to pay the creditor.
The State List did not apply in the State, and the relevant Union List entry concerning banking applied there.
The court found that transfer of property was only one of several recovery measures and was not the law's substance.
issues.conclusion: The challenged law, including its secured-debt enforcement measures, was within Parliament's legislative competence and applied in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Article 246 as applicable to the State, read with Entries 45 and 95 of List I, gives Parliament authority over banking and court jurisdiction concerning Union List matters. The pith-and-substance doctrine requires examination of the enactment as a whole rather than dissection of its provisions. The court relied on Union of India v. Delhi High Court Bar Association, (2002) 4 SCC 275, Central Bank of India v. State of Kerala, (2009) 4 SCC 94, UCO Bank v. Dipak Debbarma (decided 25 November 2016), R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, (1970) 1 SCC 248, Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for Quebec, 1947 AC 33, and A.S. Krishna v. State of Madras, 1957 SCR 399. It also applied Article 5 of the State Constitution, under which the State's legislative power extends only to matters on which Parliament lacks power to legislate for the State.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_parliamentar: A party challenges Parliament's authority to make a recovery law applicable in a specially governed State.
predicates.law_in_substance_recovers_debts_owed_to_: The law's main purpose is to facilitate recovery of debts owed to banks, even if it also provides for secured-asset transfers or other enforcement measures.
predicates.banking_subject_assigned_exclusively_to_: The applicable constitutional allocation assigns banking legislation exclusively to Parliament in the State.

issues.definition: If a challenged parliamentary law principally facilitates recovery of bank debts and banking is assigned exclusively to Parliament, Parliament may enact and apply that law.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament may provide special court jurisdiction as part of a parliamentary law on a Union subject, even where the general subject of administration of justice is not assigned to Parliament for the State.
material_facts: The challenged law provided for applications to a District Judge and appeals to the High Court in the State.
Those court provisions formed part of the statutory scheme for reviewing measures taken to recover bank debts.
The State did not apply the constitutional entry concerning administration of justice that had been relied on to challenge those provisions.

The court found that the court-jurisdiction provisions were ancillary to banking and specifically covered by the Union List entry concerning the jurisdiction and powers of courts over Union List matters.
issues.conclusion: The provisions assigning jurisdiction to the District Judge and High Court were within Parliament's legislative competence as part of the bank-debt recovery scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Entries 45 and 95 of List I, as applied to the State, support legislation concerning banking and the jurisdiction and powers of courts in relation to Union List subjects. A general legislative subject such as administration of justice does not displace a specific power to assign court jurisdiction for a Union subject. The court relied on State of Maharashtra v. Narottamdas Jethabai, (1950) 1 SCR 51, Jamshed N. Guzdar v. State of Maharashtra, (2005) 2 SCC 591, Union of India v. Delhi High Court Bar Association, (2002) 4 SCC 275, and A.S. Krishna v. State of Madras, 1957 SCR 399; it also held that the enactment should not be dissected and its parts assigned to different legislative entries.

predicates.challenge_to_court_jurisdiction_in_parli: A party challenges Parliament's authority to assign courts jurisdiction within a parliamentary statutory scheme.
predicates.provision_is_ancillary_to_union_subject: The court-jurisdiction provision supports enforcement of a matter assigned to Parliament.
predicates.courts_are_given_special_jurisdiction_fo: The law gives courts jurisdiction to review or hear matters arising from that parliamentary subject.

issues.definition: When a challenged court-jurisdiction provision supports a subject assigned to Parliament and gives courts special jurisdiction over that subject, Parliament may assign that jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A local restriction on who may acquire immovable property does not prevent a parliamentary secured-debt recovery law from operating where the rules governing enforcement sales preserve the local transfer requirements.
material_facts: The local property law restricted transfers of immovable property to persons who were not permanent residents, subject to stated exceptions.
The rule governing enforcement sales expressly made the local transfer law applicable to a person who acquires immovable property in the State.
The court found that this rule preserved the local restriction in auction sales and therefore harmonized the local law with the parliamentary recovery law.
issues.conclusion: There was no conflict that prevented the parliamentary recovery law from applying; local transfer restrictions continued to govern who could acquire property through an enforcement sale.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the rule that statutes should, where possible, be harmonized. The proviso to Rule 8(5) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 preserved the operation of the local transfer law for persons acquiring property in the State. The court further stated that, if harmonization were impossible, the parliamentary law would prevail under Article 246 as applicable to the State, read with Section 5 of the State Constitution.

predicates.parliamentary_secured_debt_sale: A parliamentary recovery law permits a secured creditor to sell property to recover a debt.
predicates.local_law_restricts_property_acquisition: A local law limits which persons may acquire immovable property in the relevant territory.
predicates.enforcement_sale_rule_preserves_local_tr: A rule governing enforcement sales makes the local transfer requirements applicable to the purchaser.

issues.definition: When a secured-debt enforcement sale is governed by a rule preserving local transfer requirements, purchasers remain subject to the local eligibility restrictions.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional protection for special rights concerning property does not bar a parliamentary recovery law where those rights are preserved and are not challenged as violating fundamental rights.
material_facts: The constitutional provision relied on protected local laws conferring special rights and privileges concerning immovable property from challenge on specified fundamental-rights grounds.
The challenge did not allege that the local property rights violated fundamental rights.
The enforcement-sale rule preserved the local transfer requirements.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional protection for special local rights did not make the parliamentary recovery law inapplicable.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the relevant constitutional protection addressed challenges based on inconsistency with fundamental rights and did not determine Parliament's legislative competence in this case. It also relied on the enforcement-sale rule's preservation of local property requirements.

predicates.challenge_to_parliamentary_recovery_law: A party argues that a parliamentary recovery law cannot apply in a territory with protected local rights.
predicates.local_property_rights_are_preserved: The governing rules continue to protect the local property-acquisition requirements.
predicates.challenge_does_not_claim_fundamental_rig: The party does not challenge the local property rights on the ground that they violate fundamental rights.

issues.definition: Where local property rights are preserved and their validity is not challenged on fundamental-rights grounds, their special constitutional protection does not itself bar a parliamentary recovery law.
